angle: The CEO asked a market question. I built an agent that answered it from our CRM data in 10 minutes
post_first_line: 10 minutes. One agent. One CEO question answered.
linkedin_post:
10 minutes. One agent. One CEO question answered.

Jeff Kirchick got a market question that would normally turn into a week-long analysis.

The CEO pointed out that the company sells an ICHRA, a healthcare benefit that works better in some states than others. Some states are friendlier to it than others.

So Jeff Kirchick built an agent to analyze the company's HubSpot data. It compared the number of quotes being run against how friendly each market is, and showed where the company is underinvesting.

The team is hiring right now, so the answer had an immediate use: a clearer sense of where to place a new hire.

The whole thing took all of 10 minutes.

The lesson is not about the agent. A CEO's question is usually a data question in disguise, and the data is already sitting in your CRM.

What question would you answer from your CRM today?

Slide 2: The company sells an ICHRA, a healthcare benefit that works better in some states.
Slide 3: Jeff Kirchick built an agent on top of the HubSpot data.
Slide 4: It compared quotes being run against how friendly each market is.
Slide 5: The output showed where the company is underinvesting in its market.
Slide 6: The team was hiring, so the answer shaped where to place someone.
Slide 7: Your CRM already holds answers to your leadership's questions.
Slide 8: What question would you answer from your CRM today?

lesson.title: Turn a CEO question into a CRM-powered answer
takeaways: Strategic questions from leadership are often questions your existing CRM data can already answer.
Comparing your activity (quotes run) against market conditions (state friendliness) exposes where you're underinvesting.
An agent can compress an analysis into about 10 minutes, which makes it usable for live decisions like hiring.
lesson.exercise: Pick one open question from your leadership team. Write down the two data sets that would answer it (for example, activity volume in your CRM versus an external market factor), then build an agent or query that compares them and bring the result to your next planning meeting.

angle: I could automate all my coaching. Here's why I walked it back.
post_first_line: Neema Zarrabian has 30 to 50 coaching rules.
linkedin_post:
Neema Zarrabian has 30 to 50 coaching rules.

That is enough to automate every coaching conversation. So why walk it back?

Neema built 7 customer stories and a long list of things reps should hit on every call. For a month, Neema made a Notion for each rep covering the questions they couldn't answer, then sent it to them directly in Slack.

It worked on paper. But nothing beats talking to a rep about a deal and watching a call together: taking notes, hearing how they phrase things, and asking why they went one direction and not another.

Neema still does some of the async version. But the core of coaching now happens live. Notes go into one-on-one docs, and the conversation covers whether the rep feels good about the approach.

The takeaway: reps are held accountable and coachable through a human conversation, not a document.

What part of coaching would you never automate?
carousel: Slide 1: Neema Zarrabian could automate all of the coaching.
Slide 2: 30 to 50 rules. 7 customer stories. Everything documented.
Slide 3: For a month, every rep got a Notion of unanswered questions.
Slide 4: Then came the call reviews: live, with notes, side by side.
Slide 5: Hearing how a rep says things shows what a doc can't.
Slide 6: Asking why they went one way beats handing over an answer.
Slide 7: Now the coaching happens live and lands in one-on-one docs.
Slide 8: Reps get held accountable through people, not documents.

lesson.title: Automate the prep, keep the coaching human
takeaways: Documenting rules and answers is easy to scale, but it doesn't replace talking through a real deal.
Watching a call with a rep shows how they say things and why they chose a direction.
Reps are held accountable and coachable through live conversation, backed by one-on-one docs.
lesson.exercise: Pick one rep's recent call this week. Watch it together, take notes, and ask why they went one direction and not another. Then log the takeaways in your one-on-one doc.

angle: How a seller with no engineering background built a working Salesforce-to-Slack-to-Gmail bot from one Claude Code session
post_first_line: Matt Stinson didn't know Apex 3 months ago.
linkedin_post:
Matt Stinson didn't know Apex 3 months ago.

Then one Claude Code session produced a working bot.

Matt Stinson described exactly what the bot should do, and the session planned out the infrastructure from there. The result: a custom Apex class in Salesforce posts a webhook that acts as the trigger. Railway hosts the interface that monitors that trigger. That pushes to a Slack bot where the end user interacts. Gmail handles the final mile, and the result flows back into Salesforce.

The backstory matters. Matt Stinson barely knew how to run customized reports in Salesforce and used to take 45 minutes on a fairly simple report.

Now the thinking is that the only real limit is having a good idea.

The skill that mattered here was describing the outcome clearly and planning the infrastructure before building. Not writing code from scratch.

What would you build if you had one session?
carousel: Slide 1: Matt Stinson didn't know Apex class code 3 months ago.
Slide 2: One Claude Code session. Described exactly what the bot should do.
Slide 3: Step one: custom Apex class in Salesforce posts a webhook trigger.
Slide 4: Step two: Railway hosts the interface monitoring that trigger.
Slide 5: Step three: a Slack bot is where the end user interacts.
Slide 6: Final mile: Gmail, then the result goes back into Salesforce.
Slide 7: A 45-minute simple report used to be the baseline.
Slide 8: The only limit now is having a good idea.

lesson.title: Plan the infrastructure, then let Claude Code build it
takeaways: Start by describing exactly what you want the tool to do, then plan the infrastructure in the same session.
A Salesforce trigger, a hosted monitor, a Slack interface, and Gmail can chain into one workflow.
Prior engineering knowledge matters less than a clear idea of the outcome.
lesson.exercise: Write a one-paragraph description of a repetitive task in your CRM, then walk through it in a Claude Code session and ask it to map the trigger, hosting, interface, and final action before building anything.

5 months changed Matt Stinson's job entirely.

angle: Ask AI what you're not thinking about. Start with one micro problem.
post_first_line: Matt Stinson's first AI workflow began with one CSV.
linkedin_post:
Matt Stinson's first AI workflow began with one CSV.

The prompt that kicked it off is the part most people skip.

Matt Stinson hadn't connected Claude or any AI tool to Salesforce yet. So the first step was to download some rep data, conversion data, and funnel data.

Then came a chat with Claude Code. The ask: tell me something I'm not thinking about. Matt Stinson shared the things already on the radar and went back and forth from there.

Somewhere in that back and forth, a pattern showed up. This could be bundled into a skill or a flow. Run it every week before a one-on-one, same process each time.

That's the move. Start on a specific micro problem, then scale it from there.

It's a good process to follow when deciding where to build in general.

What micro problem would you hand to AI first?
carousel: Slide 1: Don't start by connecting AI to everything.
Slide 2: Download some rep, conversion, and funnel data.
Slide 3: Tell Claude what you're already thinking about.
Slide 4: Then ask: what am I not thinking about?
Slide 5: Go back and forth. Let the patterns surface.
Slide 6: Spot something repeatable? Bundle it into a skill or flow.
Slide 7: Run it weekly, like before a one-on-one.
Slide 8: Start micro. Scale from there.

lesson.title: Start Micro: Find Your First AI Workflow
takeaways: Begin with real data exports, not a full integration.
Ask AI what you're not thinking about, after sharing what you are.
Repeatable patterns from the conversation become skills or flows you run on a schedule.
lesson.exercise: Export one small dataset you review regularly, share your current thinking with an AI tool, ask what you're missing, then note one part you could repeat weekly.
